sentences.text: Ceratosuchus was an extinct alligatorine crocodile that lived in North America during the latest Paleocene and earliest Eocene epochs.
Its genus name refers to the pair of flattened, triangular bony plates extending from the back of its head, which were bulbous and pointed upward.
The animal possessed a moderately-sized skull with five teeth in the premaxilla, fifteen in the maxillae, and twenty in the dentaries.
The front of the lower jaw was flattened, featuring spade-like teeth that pointed partially forward.
The discovery began when Theodore Burdosh found a knob of bone projecting from a piece of rock during an expedition.
William Bartels reported that only 5% of Clarkforkian crocodilian specimens collected by the University of Michigan could be certainly assigned to Ceratosuchus.
K. P. Schmidt named the genus Ceratosuchus in 1938 based on a skull found in Colorado.
University of Michigan paleontologists later recovered further remains from Wyoming, which were described by William Bartels in 1984.

William Bartels proposed that the small size and bluntness of the horns made them unlikely weapons or tools for threat displays, suggesting instead they were used for species recognition to distinguish Ceratosuchus from Allognathosuchus.
Bartels proposed that skull morphology and tooth wear indicate Ceratosuchus was a generalist predator of various invertebrates and vertebrates.
Traditional interpretations suggest the blunt posterior teeth were for feeding on mollusks or turtles, though Bartels noted the animals were too small for large bivalves or non-juvenile turtles.
Fossils of Ceratosuchus have been found in overbank mudstone deposits, and the animal lived between 57.5 and 51.1 million years ago during the Thanetian to Ypresian stages.
